narrative:
The model places your chance of leaving at 55%. That is just above even, but for promotion decisions it is treated as a meaningful flight risk: if you are more likely than not to depart, the organization is reluctant to invest a promotion in you.

Why? The strongest signal was your total years of experience, and it actually worked in your favor, leaning toward staying. Your 1–5 years is common among employees predicted to stay, so it did not create the departure risk. The more decisive warning came from your outside job opportunities. You indicated you have other opportunities, and among employees predicted to stay, only about one in four had the same situation. This uncommon advantage pulled the prediction toward leaving. Your sector also pushed toward leaving: working in the “other” sector is less common among stayers—roughly 22%—and made departure look somewhat more likely. Together, those upward pressures outweighed the stabilizing effect of your experience, producing the 55% leave estimate.

Because the prediction is not certain, the denial should not be treated as proof you will leave. The next step is a candid conversation: explore whether those outside opportunities are real and attractive, and identify what would make you stay. If you want to remain, focus on recognition, income fairness, emotional commitment, and reducing exhaustion. If not, a promotion may not be the right retention tool. The organization should decide whether to offer targeted support, clarify promotion criteria, or plan for succession.
